title: Opinion | What Nepal actually needs from global leaders in New York - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | What Nepal actually needs from global leaders in New York  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah is leading Nepal’s delegation to the United Nations General Assembly. This visit comes immediately after the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River caused by a rock-ice avalanche on the Langtang-Lirung mountain in Nepal. The massive floods led to the unprecedented loss of life of thousands of people, with thousands still missing, and destruction of property reaching almost $3 billion. Therefore, the high-level UN gathering has special significance for Nepal. We can use the highest global pulpit to not only highlight the catastrophic disaster in Nepal, but also create momentum for effective and transformative action on climate change and global support for reconstruction and rebuilding in Nepal.

The UN normally assesses the state of the world and reports its vision for the following year in the General Assembly. This year, the UN is focusing on issues, including global crises and conflicts, climate action, acceleration of efforts to meet the SDGs, technology and AI governance, and leadership transition.

As climate action is one of the major focus areas, Nepal should address the UN with a clear articulation of our negligible contributions to global GHG emissions, the high degree of climate change impacts due to the mountainous terrain, along with our multiple vulnerabilities and limited capacity to build resilience. We should also emphasise our own modest contributions to absorb or limit GHG emissions through afforestation and the drive for the development of renewable energy over the decades. Climate justice and enhanced global support and cooperation should find a strong resonance in the address.

At a time when the global order is fractured, and multilateral institutions are undermined, we should particularly stress that justice, interdependence, and global solidarity and cooperation are in the interests of all countries, big or small. We should underline that the national interests of all countries should be guided by values, and power should be tempered with principles. The UN was created to prevent wars, to promote peace, justice, human rights and dignity and to be a centre for harmonising global action and cooperation for economic and social development. These objectives are more relevant today in this highly interconnected and globalised world.

We should present our own initial findings and report on the massive scale and intensity of loss of life and destruction of infrastructure and property in the recent catastrophe. Likewise, the latest scientific report published by the World Weather Attribution on September 17, entitled ‘Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits’, could also be pointed out for its independent and multi-stakeholder analysis.

Similarly, the report published in 2020 by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and the UNDP Nepal can be used to emphasise the dangers of glacial lake outbursts. It identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes across the Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins, with 21 of them falling in Nepal. Since this was based on the data and research in 2019-20, there could be many more glaciers which could be in danger.

We could also link our analysis to the findings of the Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate, which was released in September 2019 by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). This was a significant report by the IPCC on melting ice and glaciers, thawing permafrost and the linkages with climate change and their impacts on water supplies and human settlements.

The UN General Assembly will help us stress the devastating climate change impacts on vulnerable countries. They are not issues for future generations; they are affecting present generations and are accelerating now.

Second, equally important are the high-level bilateral talks and pull-asides at the UNGA meetings. Nepal should make sure that there are as many bilateral talks and interactions as possible, especially with the traditional developed countries and emerging nations, whose support and cooperation are crucial for restructuring and rebuilding. No other forum brings so many world leaders together within a week at one place.

Third, due priority should be given to interactions with important mountain countries and leaders from other vulnerable groups like small island developing states, least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and other climate-vulnerable groups. We should be able to make a common cause with them and amplify the message.

Fourth, global and regional development and finance institutions are critical players in promoting sustainable development and resilience building in many countries, including in Nepal. They will be playing a very important role in the forthcoming rebuilding and reconstruction conference in Nepal. They should be clearly engaged on the sidelines of the UN meetings.

Civil society is an important part of the global advocacy efforts, especially on climate change issues. They have been the most vocal supporters for urgent and ambitious actions on emission reduction and support for vulnerable countries in general. The high-level meetings should therefore be fully utilised to garner the necessary support to make our voice louder for strengthening the cause of the mountain countries at the global forum.

It is well appreciated that the Government is hosting a high-level side event entitled ‘ Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future’ on September 25. We should make sure that it is a high-level event with strong participation of all the relevant groups as well as development partners and institutions. Coming out with a clear programme of action and follow-up events would be crucial to influence the agenda in all the relevant forums.

Finally, we should also use the UN forum to turn the disaster into an opportunity to promote our leadership role in championing the mountains and climate change. After many years of efforts, it was only during COP30 in 2025 that a dedicated dialogue on the mountains and climate change was agreed to convene for the first time by the Chair of the subsidiary bodies. In June this year, the subsidiary body held a comprehensive session in Bonn addressing climate risks, adaptation gaps, and the integration of mountain ecosystems into national instruments. There is a long way to go to mainstream the issues of mountains and climate change in the global agenda under the UNFCCC process as well as in other relevant forums. Our effective articulation now could provide us with an important opportunity to pursue this agenda further.

We should also leverage the statement that UN Secretary-General António Guterres made in his remarks on the opening day when he pointed out that the glacier melt was accelerating in Nepal, with rooftops of the world caving in and those least responsible were suffering the first and worst. He also urged the world to adopt a national plan to transition away from fossil fuels with clear timelines aligned with the 1.5C limit, and called for the implementation of the polluter-pays principle.

UNGA is not a forum where specific funding pledges are announced. But it is an important forum to sensitise the global community at the highest level on some specific concerns. The issues raised before 130 global leaders and thousands of institutional heads, businesspeople, and civil society leaders could have a major impact on the relevant meetings within the UN and beyond.

Kathmandu, Sept 24: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal held a bilateral meeting with Minister for Foreign Affairs of Iceland, Porgerour Katrin Gunnarsdottir, on the sideline of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

During the meeting, the Foreign Ministers shared perspective on the unpredictable economic and human costs resulting from climate change-related disasters including the recent devastating Bhotekoshi flood in Nepal.

They also underlined the importance of whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach for timely recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

KATHMANDU, SEPTEMBER 24

Himalayan Sherpa Club of Sonoma and the California Sherpa Association, with support from the City of Sonoma organised a fundraising event to support communities devastated by the recent floods in Nepal.

"More than $100,000 has been raised during the event which was hosted at the Sonoma Veterans Memorial Hall last night," Ang Tendi Sherpa, a member of the organizing associations said.

The event entitled "Sonoma for Nepal: A Flood Relief Charity Dinner," was attended by hundreds of community members and dignitaries and has a theme "From the Heart of Sonoma to the Peaks of Nepal," Sherpa added.

title: Nepal women’s kabaddi team seals Asian Games medal - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal women’s kabaddi team seals Asian Games medal  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s women’s kabaddi team has secured a medal at the 20th Asian Games after beating Sri Lanka 34-24 to reach the semi-finals on Thursday in Nagoya, Japan.

Teams that reach the kabaddi semi-finals are guaranteed a medal, meaning Nepal will win at least a bronze, as it did at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China.

Led by captain Manamati Bista, Nepal defeated Sri Lanka at the Tokai Citizen Gymnasium.

Nepal made a slow start but led 19-13 at half-time. The team struggled in raids but was strong in defence, where it picked up crucial points.

Nepal scored 14 points through opponents being put out, two bonus points, two from all-outs and one from super tackles.

Nepal added 15 points in the second half, while Sri Lanka managed 11.

Nepal had earlier beaten Thailand 46-43 in its opening match before losing 37-18 to Chinese Taipei.

title: Nepal participates in Japan Tourism Expo 2026 - The Tourism Times
description: Nepal participates in Japan Tourism Expo 2026  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal is participating in the four-day Japan Tourism Expo 2026 in Tokyo, with the Nepal Tourism Board leading a delegation of nine private-sector travel, trekking and hotel companies to promote Nepal in the Japanese market.

The 12th edition of the expo, which began Thursday at Tokyo Big Sight International Exhibition Centre, has brought together 1,420 companies and organisations with 1,553 booths from 74 countries and regions and all 46 prefectures of Japan. The organisers expect around 180,000 visitors during the four-day event.

The first two days, September 24 and 25, are dedicated to business-to-business (B2B) meetings, with 6,454 pre-scheduled meetings involving 855 buyers and 1,019 sellers. Business-to-consumer (B2C) activities will be held on September 26 and 27.

According to Nepal Tourism Board senior officer Pradip Gaire, Nepali companies have been holding meetings with Japanese travel agencies since the opening day, discussing tourism packages, services and travel conditions in Nepal following the recent Bhotekoshi floods. The Nepali delegation has also been providing information on the safety of tourist routes and preparations for receiving visitors.

The participating private-sector companies are Gaucheli Tours and Travels, Sumegh Tour and Travels, Himalayan Guides Nepal Treks and Expedition, Langtang Ri Trekking and Expedition, Ghale Treks and Expedition, Buddha Maya Gardens, Rupakot Resort, Chhaya Devi Complex (Aloft Kathmandu Thamel) and Gorkha International Travels. Nepal Airlines is also participating with a pavilion.

Yubaraj Gurung, another senior officer of the Tourism Board, said Nepal's participation was intended to provide information on the country's tourism situation following the floods and strengthen its presence in the Japanese market.

Nepal is promoting its Himalayan range, Lumbini, cultural heritage and biodiversity at the expo. The Nepal pavilion is providing information through audio-visual materials and brochures throughout the event.

title: Nepal disaster: 1 451 dead and 5 700 still missing one month after glacial flood - novanews.co.za
description: Nepal disaster: 1 451 dead and 5 700 still missing one month after glacial flood  novanews.co.za
publisher.title: novanews.co.za
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal – A month after a glacial collapse devastated Nepal’s border region, the country is counting its losses. Scientists link the disaster to climate change.

On August 26, a mass of ice and rock broke from Langtang Lirung’s north face at 08:37 am. The collapse began at about 5,200 metres. The section stretched more than a kilometre wide and 700 metres deep.

The debris plunged onto a glacier below before surging downhill, briefly damming the Lhende River. Consequently, water and mud burst downstream.

Geologist Sudan Bikash Maharjan, from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, said the debris travelled about 20 kilometres. It dropped 1 700 metres at Rasuwagadhi in only seven minutes.

“The elevation difference is high, within a very short length,” he told AFP. “So it just rushed down like a bullet train.”

Heavy toll

Nepal’s disaster authority says rescuers have recovered 1 451 bodies from the rubble and mud. Furthermore, more than 5 700 people remain missing.

In addition, the missing include hundreds of hydropower workers the disaster swept away. The floodwaters also overwhelmed tourists and pilgrims, whose fate remains unknown.

Identifying victims through DNA has proved a major challenge. Since morgues are overflowing, authorities have buried many bodies in mass graves after recording their DNA. However, officials have identified only about 100 bodies so far.

Meanwhile, on the Chinese side, state media have reported 43 deaths and 519 people missing. Images showed the debris obliterating a border post.

Rescue efforts

Hundreds of rescuers, many arriving by helicopter, have spent weeks digging through mud and debris. Three workers two Nepalis and a Chinese man survived in tunnels until rescuers freed them alive.

One survivor, 30-year-old Sanjay Sah, told AFP he survived 10 days in darkness by drinking muddy water and praying.

“I survived thanks to my deep faith and trust,” he said.

Aid and economic impact

The disaster has affected more than 80 000 people. As a result, thousands who lost everything are living in emergency shelters. The United Nations (UN) has launched an appeal for nearly $50 million in emergency aid.

Many communities near the epicentre remain inaccessible. Therefore, the UN and the Nepali government are delivering supplies by helicopter and cargo drone. Several countries have pledged financial support, but the total falls far short of what Nepal needs.

Nepal estimates the reconstruction bill at $4.78 billion. The country needs $57 million for short-term recovery over the next six months. In addition, the floods have cut the country’s electricity generation capacity by 10 percent. The energy sector accounts for half of all infrastructure damage.

Nepal’s economy was already under pressure before the disaster. Indeed, the World Bank estimates 82 percent of the workforce holds informal employment. GDP per capita stood at $1 447 in 2024.

Climate change link

From the first hours after the disaster, experts pointed to climate change as a contributing factor. Specifically, scientists from the World Weather Attribution group described it as a “compound crisis.” They attributed it to long-term warming, glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and geological instability.

“There is no doubt that climate change is one of the drivers,” said Friederike Otto, a professor of climate science at Imperial College London.

Therefore, Nepal’s leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a changing mountain environment. Prime Minister Balendra Shah has urged the world to recognise the dangers of climate change and act quickly.

title: Terry Mikeska Foundation supplies hope for Nepal - gosanangelo.com
description: Terry Mikeska Foundation supplies hope for Nepal  gosanangelo.com
publisher.title: gosanangelo.com
full_article:
What happens when your home country suffers a catastrophe of biblical proportions and you are thousands of miles away?

On the morning of Aug. 26, Bijaya Deuja, a nurse born and raised in Nepal who has worked in San Angelo, learned of the 5.2 earthquake and the horror of the massive Himalayan glacier collapse that triggered an avalanche and flash flood.

“I first tried to call my parents who still live there but was unable to get through," Deuja said. "I had better luck on social media where I was able to contact family. I was told that my parents and family were safe and physically intact but horribly traumatized by the disaster. As a nurse, I felt helpless knowing that I could not help.”

A life of service

In fact, Deuja is no stranger to trauma.

“My life in Nepal was always about service. I got my degree in nursing and counseling and then spent 10 years as a police officer in the Army assigned to the Peace Keeping Bureau of the United Nations," she said.

"There I worked as a counselor and nurse in Haiti during the earthquake of 2018. It has been stressful to think of the same trauma affecting people in Nepal," Deuja said.

In 2022, Deuja’s life of service also brought her to San Angelo. With a master’s degree of science in nursing, a master’s degree in political science and a master’s degree in sociology, she spent four years in surgical oncology at Shannon Medical Center in San Angelo.

“I came to the United States as the land of opportunity, and I know that so many in Nepal will never get that chance," Deuja said.

"But the people of Nepal are a hopeful people, and I have felt hopeful knowing what my friend, San Angeloan Terry Mikeska, is doing, she said. "He has been a blessing for the people of Nepal. I have never met someone so generous."

Terry Mikeska Foundation seeks to help

According to Mikeska, CEO of the Terry Mikeska Foundation, it was the disaster of the earthquake of 2015 in Nepal that inspired him to start his foundation. “I looked at the pictures of the devastation and felt like I had to do something.”

Since that first visit to Nepal 11 years ago, the foundation, through its connection with Christian groups in Nepal, has built two schools and six Christian churches, delivered more than 5,000 Bibles, hundreds of rice pots and thousands of bags of rice, including backpacks, clothing and shoes for more than 5,000 children.

The foundation has built wells and installed filtration systems, upgraded and installed restrooms, including providing feminine hygiene products to women that were often banned based on ancient Hindu traditions.

Within hours after hearing about the disaster, Mikeska had made contact with foundation volunteers on the ground.

“Pastor Amosh Khadka, one of the more than 100 Christian leaders I have recruited over the years, is on the ground now sending me photos and giving me firsthand information as to what people need the most. Here is his report from Sept. 2,” said Mikeska.

“In the flood-affected area of Bidur Municipality, Ward No. 9, Nuwakot district, impacted by the Bhote Koshi River, I have distributed essential food supplies including rice, lentils, oil, and salt, along with clothing. Thank you so much for your prayers and support that is bringing renewed hope and a fresh lease on life to these flood survivors,” Khadka said.

Mikeska said, “There is almost nothing that can be salvaged from before the flood. Everything must be purchased and brought in from neighboring areas.”

Because it is not feasible to ship goods into the area, the Terry Mikeska Foundation is now fundraising dollars for Nepal.

“Our Foundation is experienced with providing aid to Nepal and the people of San Angelo have always been generous and eager to help," Mikeska said. "We can make a difference right away.”

The website for giving is www.terrymikeskafoundation.org. Mikeska can be reached at tjmikeska@icloud.com for more information. The Foundation will continue to update its website on the status of the work and how donations have been used.

title: Heavy rain prompts travel curbs, school closures across Nepal - The Kathmandu Post
description: Heavy rain prompts travel curbs, school closures across Nepal  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Authorities in several parts of the country have imposed travel restrictions, suspended night-time transport and closed schools as the Meteorological Forecasting Division warned of heavy to extremely heavy rainfall and strong winds.

The Pathibhara Area Development Committee has urged devotees to postpone visits to the Pathibhara temple in Taplejung during the rainy spell, citing the risk of landslides and road blockages.

“Given the difficult geography and poor road conditions, travel to the area could be risky,” said committee Executive Director Prajin Hangbang. The appeal came after the weather office forecast heavy to extremely heavy rainfall and strong winds.

The District Administration Office in Chitwan has also decided to halt all traffic along the Narayanghat–Muglin road from 8pm Thursday to 5am Friday, citing the risk of floods and landslides amid continuous rainfall.

In Dang, authorities have suspended night-time transport along the Dang–Salyan section of the Rapti Highway and the Dang–Kalimati–Surkhet section of the Madan Bhandari Highway for three days from Thursday. Vehicles will not be allowed to operate from 5pm to 6am.

The District Administration Office in Ilam has imposed similar restrictions on the Mechi Highway, Mechi Corridor and other high-risk roads. Night-time traffic will be prohibited from 7 pm to 5 am through Sunday morning.

The weather warning has also disrupted educational activities. Raksirang and Indrasarowar rural municipalities in Makawanpur have announced a two-day school holiday on Thursday and Friday. Raksirang chair Raj Kumar Malla said the closure was necessary as students and teachers in the remote municipality have to cross streams and rivers to reach schools.

In Salyan, all schools in Sharada and Bagchaur municipalities will remain closed on Thursday and Friday. Other local governments in the district are also considering school closures from Friday depending on weather conditions.

The Meteorological Forecasting Division has urged people already in mountainous areas for trekking to return to safer locations and those planning trips to postpone them. It has also advised the public to avoid long-distance travel amid the risk of floods and landslides from continuous rainfall expected through Sunday.

The adverse weather has also forced the Janamat Party to postpone its general convention. The convention, scheduled for Friday and Saturday at Birgunj Town Hall, will now be held on Saturday, October 3, according to party spokesperson Chandan Singh.

title: Departure from norm - Nepali Times
description: Departure from norm  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
When Prime Minister Balendra Shah departed from Kathmandu on Tuesday on a scheduled Qatar Airways flight, there was no guard of honour, no diplomats and officials lining up to say bye, no imported gladioli to be handed to the bodyguard, no motorcade with flashing lights bringing him to the ramp below the plane.

He stepped out of his limo onto the tarmac in his signature all-black attire, shades and Goldstar shoes. Shook hands with Home Minister Sudan Gurung. And that was it.

This low-key departure was universally lauded, even from those usually critical of the RSP ministers pulling off populist stunts.

This was a deliberate departure from the grandiose pomp and ceremony displayed by his predecessors before and after foreign visits. Even the PM’s entourage was minimalist: Chief Adviser Kumar Byanjankar (Ben), his personal secretary and the foreign secretary, security detail, and a photographer. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal had left for New York with his own small team a few days prior.

This has been Shah’s branding in the seven months he has been in office: to show that he is different from the old leaders.

Prime Minister Shah was received in Doha at the airport by Qatar’s Minister of Transport Jassim Saif Ahmed Al-Sultani, and was seen in videos being transported via airport buggy with Kumar Ben in his trademark shirt to catch his connecting flight to JFK.

But this attempt to avoid fanfare on departure was in sharp contrast to how his followers on social media portrayed his arrival in New York. Balen fans at home and abroad created a narrative of a wild welcome for their dear leader in New York. AI-generated videos and real clips of other world leaders cruising down Fifth Avenue to cheering crowds were captioned as being for Nepal’s prime minister.

AI AND FAKE CLIPS

Fake photos of Shah being personally received by President Donald Trump at JFK went bacterial on the web, as supporters and even mainstream media who did not know any better, shared it. Videos of Trump sounding the opening bell for the stock market in the Oval Office in July as well as clips of the bell rung at the UN General Assembly floor to mark the beginning of this year’s session were jubilantly shared as representing the RSP’s bell election symbol.

Nepalis need another reminder that the country should not have an inflated sense of its own geopolitical importance. The best way for supporters to prove their backing for Balen may be to let him be who he wants to be.

full_article:
Heavy rain and snowfall began across Nepal on Wednesday evening, as forecasters had warned, prompting authorities to step up preparations after a series of deadly floods and landslides earlier this year.

The government has urged people to remain vigilant, particularly between September 25 and 27, when the weather system is expected to bring heavy to extremely heavy rain, thunderstorms, lightning and strong winds across much of the country.

So far, there have been no reports of significant loss of life or damage from the latest spell. Authorities have, however, restricted night-time travel on major highways because of the risk of landslides and flooding. Much of Nepal’s road network cuts through steep, landslide-prone hills.

People living near rivers have also been warned to remain alert and be ready to move to safer ground if water levels rise.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said heavy rain could cause flooding, soil erosion, landslides and debris flows, with urban areas and the southern plains particularly vulnerable. It also warned of heavy snowfall at high altitude and possible disruption to flights and road transport.

The warnings have been closely heeded after the devastation caused by recent floods and landslides, with authorities and tourism agencies urging people to avoid unnecessary travel.

The immediate impact, however, has been felt most sharply in the mountains.

Autumn is Nepal’s main trekking and mountaineering season, but expeditions on several of the world’s highest peaks have been halted before climbers could make their summit attempts.

Nepal issued 579 climbing permits for 10 mountains this autumn, including 493 for Manaslu and 34 for Dhaulagiri. The permits brought the government about $1.5 million in royalties.

The disruption comes as Nepal’s tourism industry is still trying to regain momentum after the Covid-19 pandemic. Autumn is traditionally one of the busiest periods for trekking, and prolonged rain and snow could lead to cancellations and further losses for guides, trekking agencies, hotels and other businesses.

The Expedition Operators’ Association Nepal has issued an urgent safety warning to expedition organisers, advising them to move climbers and high-altitude workers to safer locations amid forecasts of heavy snowfall and strong winds across the Himalayas.

The association urged operators to assess weather risks immediately and ensure that foreign climbers, Nepali guides, support staff and base-camp personnel are moved to designated safe areas or brought down to lower altitudes. The warning applies to ongoing expeditions on major peaks, including Manaslu and Dhaulagiri.

The Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal has separately advised its members and adventure tourists not to begin new trekking or mountaineering trips between September 25 and 27. Trekkers and support crews already on routes or in exposed areas such as riverbanks, steep slopes and landslide-prone terrain have been urged to stop travelling and move to safer locations.

The Nepal Tourism Board has issued a similar travel advisory.

The weather is being driven by a low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal. Senior mountain meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar said south or south-easterly winds associated with the system were carrying moisture northwards towards the Indian plains and Nepal.

“Heavy weather is thus expected during this period, 25-27 September, over Nepal, most notably from the Dhaulagiri range eastwards over the entire mountain range, including the high Himalayas and the Terai plains,” he said.

The warnings have helped climbers decide against making summit attempts after completing their acclimatisation rotations.

Forecast agencies have continued to update their predictions, but even an improvement after September 27 may not be enough to salvage the mountaineering season.

Mingma Gyalje Sherpa, renowned mountaineer known as Mingma G, said prolonged snowfall could make the upper mountains inaccessible for weeks.

“Yes, it is possible, but the weather we are expecting will not allow us to reach even base camp for three to four weeks. You can imagine two metres of snow at base camp. Sherpas can’t break a trail through such huge snow,” he said.

The problem would not end with reaching base camp. Heavy snowfall could bury fixed ropes on the upper mountain, forcing rope-fixing teams to reopen the route to the summit before climbers could attempt a final ascent.

Recent disasters have also changed how climbers and expedition organisers assess the risks.

“The Broad Peak avalanche made everyone respond on time. The Rasuwa flood may be another reason to respond, and we all know the snow on Manaslu,” Mingma said.

Many climbers are now returning home. Some face work commitments, while others have been persuaded to leave after receiving warnings from relatives concerned about the deteriorating weather.

“Most of them have to return because of their work commitments, and many are returning because of news about bad weather, as they get calls from their families,” he said.
